text: Franklin Mitchell Beamer, born on October 18, 1946, is an American former college football player and coach, best known for his tenure with the Virginia Tech Hokies. He played as a defensive cornerback for Virginia Tech from 1966 to 1968 and earned 11 varsity letters in football, basketball, and baseball during his high school years in Hillsville, Virginia. After graduating from Virginia Tech in 1969 with Omicron Delta Kappa distinction, he served as an assistant football coach at Radford High School while attending Radford University for graduate school. Beamer began his coaching career as a graduate assistant at the University of Maryland in 1972, then worked at The Citadel under Bobby Ross for seven seasons, including two as defensive coordinator. In 1979, he was hired as defensive coordinator at Murray State under Mike Gottfried, and in 1981, he was promoted to head coach, compiling a record of 42–23–2 (.642) over six seasons. He was hired as head coach at Virginia Tech on December 22, 1986, replacing Bill Dooley, who had resigned due to NCAA violations. Beamer signed a four-year contract worth $80,000 annually and took over a program that had reached six bowl games prior to his arrival. Due to sanctions from the NCAA, the Hokies were limited to 85 total scholarships in 1988 and 1989 and 17 initial scholarships in 1989, resulting in a combined 5–17 record in 1987 and 1988. His record from 1993 to 2011 was 185–58 (.761), and from 1993 to 2015, the Hokies went to postseason play every season, achieving 23 consecutive bowl appearances. The team won three Big East championships and four ACC titles, with Beamer named Big East Coach of the Year in 1995, 1996, and 1999, and ACC Coach of the Year in 2004 and 2005. The Hokies achieved a 11–0 regular season in 1999, earning a spot in the 2000 Sugar Bowl against Florida State, where they lost 46–29 despite leading 29–28 in the fourth quarter. Virginia Tech had its second straight 11-win season in 2000, which was rated as the best season in school history by College Football Reference and remains so in 2023. In 2004, the Hokies won the ACC Championship in their first season in the league, and from 2005 to 2011, they won at least 10 games each season, a feat unmatched in the country. Beamer's overall record at Virginia Tech was 238–121–2 (.663) over 29 seasons, and he was the winningest active coach in Division I FBS at the time of his retirement with 280 career victories, ranking sixth in history. He retired on November 1, 2015, after a final regular season win over Virginia, and his last game was a 55–52 victory over Tulsa in the Independence Bowl on December 26. Memphis' Justin Fuente replaced him as head coach at the end of the 2015 season. Beamer was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 2018. He was born in Mount Airy, North Carolina, and grew up on a farm in Fancy Gap, Virginia. He is a direct descendant of the Allen clan of Carroll County, Virginia; in 1912, his great-uncle Floyd Allen fired rounds during a courtroom shooting that killed five people, including the judge, prosecutor, and sheriff. In 1953, at age seven, Beamer suffered a severe accident when a smoldering broom ignited a gasoline can, resulting in burns to his shoulders, chest, and right neck. He underwent dozens of skin graft procedures and was left with permanent scarring. After retiring from coaching, Beamer accepted an eight-year position as a special assistant to Whit Babcock, director of athletics at Virginia Tech, focusing on athletic development and advancement. On January 17, 2017, he was appointed to the College Football Playoff Committee, becoming the 14th member of the 13-member panel formed in 2013, serving a three-year term. On August 6, 2015, Virginia Tech renamed Spring Road to Beamer Way in honor of him, and the athletics department changed its mailing address to 25 Beamer Way, commemorating his jersey number. In 2016, the team began honoring Beamer by selecting a special teams player each week to wear the number 25 jersey, a tradition that continued beyond 2016. On February 4, 2016, Governor Terry McAuliffe declared Frank Beamer Day in Virginia. On October 6, 2018, Virginia Tech renamed its indoor practice facility to the Beamer–Lawson Indoor Practice Facility and unveiled a permanent bronze statue of Beamer on Moody Plaza. On May 11, 2023, Beamer received the Ut Prosim Medal, the university's highest honor, recognizing service, sacrifice, generosity, and accomplishment. Beamer married Cheryl Oakley on April 1, 1972, after meeting on a blind date while he was a senior at Virginia Tech; they have two children, Shane and Casey, and six grandchildren. Shane Beamer, who played long snapper at Virginia Tech in 1999, served as running backs coach and associate head coach at Virginia Tech from 2011 to 2015 before joining the University of Georgia, then Oklahoma University, and is currently the head coach at the University of South Carolina. In 2006, Beamer and Cheryl published the children's book Yea, It's a Hokie Game Day! under Mascot Books, Inc. After the April 16, 2007, Virginia Tech shooting, Beamer became a prominent voice in the community, stating that the university should not be defined by one act of violence, emphasizing the importance of caring and thoughtfulness. Shane Beamer served as acting head coach for the 2014 Military Bowl.
